p: Monday, April 5, Maria got to the fourth floor at 6:30 with two breakfast burritos from the truck on Mulberry and one word at the top of her legal pad. KIRAN, in capitals, underlined twice. The light in the analysts' room was already on.

Kiran had a document open on both monitors. Request for Proposal, One Chart implementation services and integration platform. Eighty-one pages. The file said he'd last saved it at 1:14 Sunday morning.
She set a burrito on his keyboard, on top of section four. Eat that. Then tell me how many hours you worked last week.

I don't really count them. I know. Starting today, I do. She pulled a chair over. Procurement writes the RFP. That's Pam Castillo's job, and she's good at it. You write the requirements, because nobody knows them better. And you leave at five.
He unwrapped the burrito slowly, like it might be a trick. Five's early. Five is when the day ends. I looked it up. He ate half of it, which she counted as a start.

Tuesday at 7:30 Ochoa didn't wait for her one-page status. The board said a recommendation by summer. Summer's too late. If One Chart goes live in October, a partner has to be on the ground in Cheyenne by June. You've got six weeks to do what usually takes six months.

None of them. You make each one shorter. You don't make any of them disappear. He turned his coffee cup a quarter turn, which he did when he was deciding how much to say. I've signed a lot of these contracts. I'd like the last few to be ones I never have to explain.
She noticed the last few. She didn't ask. On her phone, unopened since Friday night, was Brett Talbot's dinner invitation, two exclamation points and all.
Ochoa's Legal Pad: how to buy something you'll live with.

Sunday morning at the Greeley diner, Ochoa wrote six words down the side of the legal pad and numbered them. There's a ballgame today, he said. I'd guess somebody offered you a suite. We'll get to that.

A selection runs in order. Requirements come first, from the gap analysis. Then a request for information, an RFI: a short question to the market. Who can do this, how, and roughly what does it cost? It commits nobody. Then a request for proposal, an RFP, goes to the vendors who can: your requirements, your scripts, your contract terms, and a firm price, due on a date. A request for quotation, an RFQ, is for when you know exactly what you want and only need a price. After that come demos, site visits, references, scoring, negotiation, and the contract. Bid it competitively, unless your policy allows a sole source and you can write down why.
How the exam asks it. If the organization doesn't know the market yet, the answer is an RFI. If it knows its requirements and wants offers it can compare and hold vendors to, it's an RFP.

A nondisclosure agreement, an NDA, protects confidential information you share, like network diagrams and interface lists. Sign it before you share, and share only what the other side needs. A business associate agreement, a BAA, is the contract HIPAA requires before a vendor creates, receives, keeps, or sends protected health information for you. A bidder looking at your architecture needs an NDA. A vendor touching patient data needs a BAA. Run demos on test patients, and nobody needs PHI to bid.

A statement of work, an SOW, says what the vendor will deliver: tasks, deliverables, milestones, who does what, and how each deliverable is accepted. A service level agreement, an SLA, says how well a service has to perform: availability, response and fix times by severity, how it's measured, and what happens when it's missed. That usually means service credits, and a right to leave after repeated misses.
How the exam asks it. Match the document to the job. Sharing secrets calls for an NDA, PHI calls for a BAA, defining the work calls for an SOW, and measuring performance calls for an SLA.

A selection committee needs the people who'll live with the choice and the people who can judge each part of it. Clinicians who'll use the system judge workflow. The CMIO or CNIO speaks for clinical content and safety. The interface engineer judges whether it'll connect. The CISO judges the vendor's security controls. The privacy officer judges how patient data will be handled, and the BAA. Finance checks cost, procurement runs the process and keeps it fair, and legal reads the contract. The IT leader chairs, and writes down before the first demo who scores what.
How the exam asks it. Expect to match a role to what it evaluates. Each one judges what it's accountable for. A committee made only of IT, or only of executives, is the wrong answer.

Never let a vendor run its own demo. Write scripts from your requirements, real work with test patients, give every vendor the same ones ahead of time, and score each script as it runs, before anyone talks.

While it runs, watch what the screen does for the clinician. Does the information show up where the work already happens, labeled so a nurse can trust it, with the next step one click away? A feature in a tab nobody opens doesn't exist at three in the morning, Ochoa said.

Then check the claims. Site visits go to organizations like yours, chosen by you, at your expense. Talk to the people who use it with the vendor out of the room. Ask for the whole client list, and call a customer who left. Set the scoring weights before the first demo, and don't touch them after you've seen who's winning.

How the exam asks it. The best demo is scripted, live, and the same for everyone. The best reference is one you chose. Judge clinical functionality by whether it fits the point of care, not whether the data exists somewhere.

Everything a vendor promised in a demo is a sales claim until it's in the contract. Attach the requirements, the RFP response, and the demo scripts as exhibits. Write acceptance tests from them, and tie payments to passing. Later, you'll validate what was delivered against what was contracted and designed, and you can only do that if it's written down.

Then read for five things. Cost: price holds, what's included, what isn't. Schedule: milestones and named key people. Support and maintenance: hours, upgrades, response times. Performance: SLAs with remedies. And the way out: termination rights, your data and configuration returned in standard formats, and help moving to whoever's next. Compare total cost of ownership over five years, never the license line alone.
How the exam asks it. When a vendor promises something, the best answer puts it in the contract with a test. Best efforts and good faith aren't standards. Compare vendors on five-year TCO.

Ochoa tapped the pad. For six weeks, every vendor in this race is going to be very nice to you. Gifts, meals, tickets, and travel from a bidder during a selection create a conflict of interest, or the look of one, and in procurement those cost the same. Follow the gift policy, which during an active selection usually means decline and disclose the offer.

A personal conflict, like a job offer or a relative at a bidder, gets disclosed in writing, and that person steps out of scoring the vendor involved. Every bidder gets the same information on the same day, through one contact in procurement. No bidder ever learns another's price. He tore the page off. You can be friends with a vendor. You can't owe one.

How the exam asks it. For gifts during a selection, decline and disclose. For a personal conflict, disclose and recuse from that vendor. Fairness means equal information and equal access for every bidder.

Pam Castillo had run Cascade's purchasing for eleven years and read contracts for fun, by her own account. She'd printed Kiran's draft and come up to the fourth floor with it under one arm and a pencil behind her ear.

It's a good RFP, she said. For the implementation partner, we know who's out there. Corvane's own services team, and a couple of consulting firms that have done Corvane go-lives. For the integration platform, I don't know who's out there. I don't think you do either.
Marcus knew of two companies that sold a cloud FHIR platform. Kiran had found nine on an industry list. Some of the nine probably couldn't talk to a MedaLink built in 2012. Nobody knew which.
A. Send Kiran's full RFP to all nine platform companies today, to save time.
B. Buy Corvane's own integration add-on without a bid, since time is short.
C. Send a short RFI to all nine now, then an RFP to those who qualify.
D. Ask Brett which platforms work best with Corvane, and invite only those.

Pam has a five-page RFI out by Wednesday noon. What do you sell, who runs it, have you ever connected to MedaLink, what does it roughly cost, and name two customers, due in a week. Kiran's requirements go into the RFP that follows. Six of the nine answer, and three can do the work. Pam sends Kiran a note, and he prints it and pins it above his desk. Best requirements I've seen in eleven years. Go home.

That's the move. A request for information surveys a market you don't know yet. It's short, it binds nobody, and it tells you who should get the request for proposal, which asks for a firm offer you can compare and hold them to.
Wednesday Pam asked for the selection committee's names by Friday. The list on Maria's legal pad had started at four, all from IT, and it kept growing.

Walt Hagen had heard about the selection from Renee, and he called before Maria could call him. I hear you're buying the thing I'll use for the rest of my career, he said. Do I get a vote, or a survey?
Aisha wanted a seat. So did Gail, who'd said so in an email with no greeting. Nate wanted the vendors' security answers before anybody saw a demo. Ochoa wanted it done in six weeks.
A. Name nine members, each scoring the part they own, with roles in writing.
B. Keep the committee to IT, so it moves fast and speaks one language.
C. Have Ochoa and Glenn choose the vendors, with the committee advising.
D. Seat everyone who asks to join, and have each score vendors on everything.

Nine chairs. Walt and Gail score clinical workflow, for the people who'll use it. Aisha scores clinical content and safety, as CMIO. Marcus scores whether it'll connect. Nate scores security, and Joan scores how patient data is handled. Glenn's analyst checks cost, Pam runs the process, and Maria chairs. It's on one page by Friday: who scores what. Walt reads to the bottom and taps the line with his name on it. A vote, he says. On the clicks. Fine.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. A good committee brings the roles that will live with the choice and the roles that can judge each part of it. Clinicians judge workflow. The CMIO judges content. The interface engineer, the CISO, and the privacy officer each judge what they answer for. Put the roles in writing before the first demo.

The RFI answers came back Tuesday, April 13. Three integration platforms could do the work, among them Tributary, which ran in its own cloud, and Sandhill, which installed on Cascade's servers. Two firms would bid the implementation: Corvane's services team, and Ridgeline Health Partners, a Denver consulting firm with four Corvane go-lives behind it. Pam would send the RFP on Friday.

Marcus came to Maria's office with a printout he wouldn't put down. Every Relay interface, all two hundred and twelve, with addresses, ports, and the network diagram for the three Wyoming hospitals. They can't price the work without this. And I don't send this to anybody. It's a map of how to get into us.
Joan was copied on his email. She replied in four minutes. Before anything leaves the building, tell me what's in it.
A. Leave the inventory out, and let bidders estimate from a single total count.
B. Have every bidder sign an NDA first, and share only what bidding needs.
C. Require an NDA and a BAA from every bidder before anyone gets the RFP.
D. Send the full inventory with the RFP to all five bidders, marked confidential.

Pam has her standard mutual nondisclosure agreement signed by all five by Thursday night. Marcus cuts the printout to what a bidder needs to price the work: interfaces by type, message volumes, and the standard each one uses. No addresses, no ports. Joan reads the RFP and stops at one line. Demos will use test patients only. Then nobody needs patient data to bid, she says. The BAA comes with the contract, for whoever wins.

Exactly right. An NDA protects confidential business information, like network details, so sign it before you share, and share the minimum. A BAA is a different paper. HIPAA requires it when a vendor will handle PHI, so it comes with the contract, not the bid.
Friday, April 16, the RFP went out at nine. At 4:40 an email came in from a familiar address.

An email from Brett Talbot. Subject: Rockies Sunday?. Maria! Corvane has the suite at Coors Field Sunday, and two seats just opened up. Bring Lucia. Bring Ray Ochoa if he'll come. No business, I promise, just baseball. And the dinner offer stands, any night next week. Brett
Corvane's services team had held the RFP since nine that morning. Lucia had never sat in a suite. Maria had, once, at a Penwright launch party, and she still remembered the shrimp.
A. Go, since Corvane is already the EHR vendor and a ballgame decides nothing.
B. Go, but pay face value for the two seats, so it isn't really a gift.
C. Decline in writing, tell Pam about the offer, and remind the committee of the rule.
D. Turn down the tickets, but go to the dinner, since it's a business meal.

She writes Brett two warm lines. Thank you, and no, not while Corvane is bidding, and the same goes for dinner. She forwards the offer to Pam, who logs it. Then she sends the committee one sentence: no gifts, meals, or side calls with any bidder until the contract is signed, and every question goes through Pam. Brett answers in ten minutes. Totally understand. Had to ask. My boss asks if I asked. Lucia understands less. You turned down free Rockies tickets? For ethics? For ethics. Huh.

That's the move. Decline gifts from a bidder during a selection, disclose the offer under the gift policy, and hold the whole committee to the same rule. One point of contact in procurement keeps every bidder's access equal.

Tuesday, April 20, the committee met in the big room on the second floor to write the demo scripts. Each script was a real piece of work with a test patient. A Laramie discharge. A Cheyenne heparin drip. A Rawlins lab result headed for the emergency department. An interface failing at 3 AM. Maria had written the first one herself.
A Rawlins patient, transferred to Greeley, with twenty-three active medications. Show every one arriving. Show where the nurse sees them.
Why twenty-three? Walt asked. Why not twenty?

Because MedaLink stops at twenty, Maria said. She put Kiran's count on the screen. Last year 61 patients came to Greeley or Fort Collins from Cheyenne, Laramie, or Rawlins with more than twenty active medications. Every one of their transfer summaries listed exactly twenty, and none of them said anything was missing. The receiving nurse can't tell a short list from a cut one. I've seen what a missing page does. She stopped there.
Walt looked at her for a moment, then at the screen. Sixty-one, he said. Put it first. Nobody argued. The committee voted script one in as written.
Walt caught her at the door. You stopped yourself in there. I did. Good. I can vote on sixty-one.
In the car she understood she'd had the whole night ready, and hadn't needed it. The story wasn't for a committee. It never had been.
Pam's email was waiting the next morning. Two vendors had already asked to run their own standard demos instead. It would save everyone time, they said.
A. Give every vendor the same scripts and test patients, scored live.
B. Send the scripts, and let each vendor pick the ones that fit its time.
C. Ask for recorded demos the committee can watch on its own schedule.
D. Let each vendor run its standard demo, so every one shows its best work.

Pam sends all twelve scripts and the test patients to all five bidders the same morning, with the rules. Run them in order, live, in a test system, no slides. Each member scores the scripts they own as they happen, on paper, before anybody talks. Walt asks for a clicker counter. Kiran buys him one at a sporting goods store on his lunch break, and Maria counts it as a lunch break.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Scripted demos, written from your requirements, run live on test data, the same for every vendor, are the core of a fair selection. Score each script while you watch it, before discussion, so the loudest voice doesn't set the score.

Monday, May 3, Tributary ran script one at 9:15. Tributary sold a cloud FHIR platform, and its RFP answers had been the strongest of the three. Its lead engineer pulled up a test patient at Rawlins with twenty-three medications and transferred her to Greeley on the screen.

All twenty-three arrived. The room let out a breath. Then Gail asked where her nurses would find them, and the engineer clicked into a tab called Outside Records, three levels below the admission screen. The medication reconciliation the nurses used every day still showed nothing.

My nurses won't find that, Gail said. Not at three in the morning. The engineer said the tab could be configured. Maria looked at the twenty-three lines, every one present, in a place nobody would look.
A. Score script one as passed, since all twenty-three medications arrived.
B. Add a pop-up telling nurses to open the Outside Records tab on admission.
C. Have outside meds go straight onto the active med list when patients arrive.
D. Require outside meds in the nurse's own reconciliation, labeled, with gaps flagged.

Maria rewrites the script's pass line on the spot. Outside medications appear inside the admission reconciliation, each labeled with the sending hospital and when it was last updated, ready to continue or stop. If the sending system says its list was cut short, a banner says so at the top. Tributary's engineer makes a call at the break and comes back. We can do the banner if MedaLink sends a count. Corvane does the rest. Marcus nods. MedaLink sends a count. I'll show you where.

Exactly right. Functionality helps clinicians when it puts the right data in the workflow they already use, labeled so they can trust it, with the next step built in. Medication reconciliation at transfer is where missing data hurts people, so make completeness visible.

Tributary's three references had come with its RFP response, each one glowing. A university hospital in Ohio. A children's hospital in Texas. A forty-hospital system in the Southeast. All three were large and urban, and none ran anything like MedaLink.
Marcus had one question about all of them. Who answers their phone at two in the morning? Those places have twenty engineers on nights. We have me.
Tributary had also offered a site visit to its showcase customer, all expenses paid.
A. Call the three references Tributary provided, and ask each about support.
B. Get the full client list, pick small rural sites, and visit one on your own.
C. Skip the references, since the scripted demos already showed enough.
D. Take the showcase visit Tributary offered, since it's paid for and set up.

Pam asks for every Tributary customer. Maria picks three that look like Wyoming, small hospitals with old systems, plus one that left Tributary last year. Marcus and Gail drive to a 25-bed hospital in western Nebraska on Wednesday, on Cascade's dime, and talk to the interface analyst and two night nurses with nobody from Tributary in the room. The analyst likes the platform. Help desk is great, eight to five Mountain. At two in the morning you get a voicemail. The customer that left says the same thing. Marcus writes it down and draws a box around it.

That's the move. References and site visits work when you choose them. Pick organizations like yours, talk to the people who use it with the vendor out of the room, and call a former customer. Pay your own way, so the visit isn't a gift.
Thursday at 7 AM Marcus was waiting outside Maria's office, which he had never done. He came in and shut the door, which he'd also never done.

At Monday's demo, during the break, Tributary's lead engineer had found him at the coffee urn. They'd talked HL7 for twenty minutes, happily. Then the engineer mentioned that Tributary was hiring someone to run support for its Mountain region, and named a salary.
Twice what I make, Marcus said. I didn't say yes. I didn't say no. And I've been scoring their scripts all week. He looked at his hands. Nobody calls a guy my age.
Then, because he was Marcus, he added one more thing. I'm telling you because you'd have told me.
A. Record it, recuse him from scoring Tributary, keep his know-how.
B. Thank him, and keep him scoring, since he hasn't accepted anything.
C. Take Marcus off the selection committee entirely, just to be safe.
D. Disqualify Tributary for approaching a member of the selection committee.

Maria writes it up with him in ten minutes, and Pam files it with the committee record. His Tributary scores come out of the matrix. He still answers technical questions about every other bidder, in writing, where the whole committee can read them. Pam reminds all bidders not to approach committee members. Marcus stops at the door. Ten years ago I'd have taken the call and not told anybody. What's different? He thinks about it. Somebody here would notice I was gone.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. A conflict of interest has to be disclosed and managed. Put it in writing, recuse the person from decisions involving that vendor, and keep the record. The disclosure is the ethical act. The recusal protects both the decision and the person.

Friday, May 7, Pam put the implementation partner scores on the screen. Corvane's services team, 3.85. Ridgeline Health Partners, 3.75. The weights had been set and signed by all nine members on April 20, before anyone saw a demo.

Corvane had converted MedaLink hospitals six times. Ridgeline had done four Corvane go-lives and no MedaLink conversions. But Ridgeline had sent a nurse educator who spent the whole break with Gail, and Corvane had sent a project manager who got the name of Gail's hospital wrong twice.
Their team was better, and you know it, Gail said. Raise the team weight from fifteen to twenty-five. Take it out of conversion record. We learned something in those demos.
Pam ran it while they watched. On Gail's weights, Ridgeline won by four tenths.
A. Call it a tie within the margin, and ask both firms for one more demo.
B. Keep the agreed weights, and put Gail's concern into the winner's contract.
C. Change the weights as Gail asks, since the demos taught them something real.
D. Let Ochoa decide, since the scores are too close to call by the numbers.

Maria says it plainly. The weights stand, because they were set before anyone knew who'd win. Gail's point is real, so it goes into Corvane's statement of work: named key people for Wyoming, a nurse educator on site at all three hospitals, and Cascade's right to ask for a new project manager. Gail folds her arms. Walt speaks before she can. I count clicks for a living. You don't move the finish line after the race. Gail looks at him a long time. Fine. I want the educator by name.

Exactly right. Weighted scoring is fair only when the weights are set before evaluation and applied the same way to every vendor. When the process turns up a real concern, deal with it in negotiation and the contract, not by re-scoring.
Monday, May 10, Corvane's draft statement of work arrived at seven in the morning, forty pages, and Walt had read it by nine. He called from the surgeons' lounge in Laramie.

I counted their discharge at the demo. Forty-four clicks. Our requirement is forty-one. Their man said they'd get it down in the build. Page twelve says they'll configure the system to Corvane's standard build and best practices. Where in here does it say forty-one?
It didn't. Nowhere in forty pages did the draft mention the requirements, the twelve scripts, or anything Corvane had written in its RFP answers.
A. Hold back a fifth of Corvane's fee until Walt says he's satisfied.
B. Add a line that Corvane will make its best efforts to meet the click target.
C. Accept the SOW as written, and trust Corvane to cut the clicks in the build.
D. Attach the requirements and scripts, with acceptance tests before payments.

Pam sends the change back by noon. The requirements list, the twelve scripts, and Corvane's own RFP answers become exhibits to the contract. Each milestone has acceptance tests drawn from them, and each payment follows a pass. A routine discharge in forty-one clicks or fewer is test 7.3. Walt calls back at 4:15. Seven point three, he says. I'll be there when they run it.

That's the move. You can only validate a system against the contract and design specs if they're in the contract. Attach the requirements and the vendor's proposal as exhibits, write acceptance tests from them, and tie payment to passing.
Decision eleven. Two in the morning.

Tributary's contract came Monday afternoon. It was short and well written, and on page nine it promised to use commercially reasonable efforts to keep the platform available. Support ran eight to five Mountain, Monday to Friday, with after-hours help for an added fee.
Nate had read it before Maria had. Commercially reasonable means whatever they did last month, he said. Ask Marcus what the Nebraska analyst told him.
Marcus didn't have to look it up. Two in the morning, you get a voicemail.
A. Ask Tributary for a ten percent discount in place of the SLA terms.
B. Buy the after-hours support add-on, and leave the rest as written.
C. Write a real SLA: uptime, response times, credits, and an exit.
D. Sign it as written, since the price is good and the platform did well.

Nate and Pam work it out with Tributary's lawyer over two calls. Availability of 99.9 percent each month, measured by Cascade's monitoring as well as theirs. A person answering a severity one call within fifteen minutes, any hour. Service credits when they miss, and the right to leave after three misses in six months. A disaster recovery plan, attached as an exhibit. Tributary fights the credits and loses. Nate reads the final draft. Better, he says, and initials every page.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Vendor contracts need measurable performance terms: availability, response and fix times by severity, how they're measured, remedies like service credits, and a right to end the contract for repeated failure. Support hours should match when patients need the system, which is always.
Tuesday, May 11, the last open item was Marcus's. He'd written it on a sticky note and stuck it to her monitor at six that morning. What happens to our feeds if Tributary gets bought, or goes broke?
Tributary was six years old and had raised money three times. Its standard contract said either side could leave on ninety days' notice. It didn't say what Cascade would leave with.
A. Accept the ninety-day clause, since either side can leave on notice.
B. Sign for one year only, so Cascade can leave easily if things go wrong.
C. Ask for the platform's source code to be put in escrow, in case they fail.
D. Require its data and mappings back in standard formats, plus help leaving.

Pam adds a page. Cascade owns its data and every mapping and configuration it pays Tributary to build. If the contract ends for any reason, Tributary returns all of it in standard formats, FHIR resources and documented mappings, with six months of paid transition help. Cascade gets notice of any sale of the company, and the contract survives the sale. Marcus reads the page slowly, then peels his sticky note off her monitor and puts it in his pocket.

Exactly right. Good vendor contracts plan the exit: who owns the data and configuration, how it comes back and in what format, transition help, and what happens if the vendor is sold or fails. It's cheapest to negotiate while they still want to sign.

Tuesday, May 11, at 4:10 PM, Ochoa signed two contracts at the round table in his office, with Glenn's initials already on every page. Corvane's services team would lead the conversion at Cheyenne, Laramie, and Rawlins. Tributary would carry the FHIR feeds. Five weeks, inside Ochoa's six.

Brett called at 4:30. I want you to know something, he said. That was the hardest sale I've made in nine years, and the cleanest. My boss asked me who you were. He laughed, and then he didn't. This one makes my year, Maria. I won't let it go sideways. She believed he meant it. She also had the contract.

On the walk back to her office she added it up. Five weeks of slowing down on purpose. A short letter before a long one. A script before a show. An NDA before a map, weights before scores, and a page about leaving before the pages about starting. None of it was fast, and all of it was faster than doing it over. Every promise anyone had made in a demo was in a contract now, with a test number beside it.

Lucia had sent her deposit to the nursing program in Greeley on May 1, after three weeks of a matrix taped to the refrigerator that Maria wasn't allowed to touch. It was still there that night. Six criteria, two schools, and a column of weights that had been crossed out and rewritten.

You changed your weights, Maria said. After the visits. Yeah. At work, that gets a contract protested. Lucia shrugged. I wanted to see what I already wanted. Turned out it was Greeley. She tapped the last row, added in pen. It said: where Mom started. I want to do my clinicals where you did yours.

Maria looked at the row a long time. The charge desk. The hallway outside it, at three in the morning, her first year. That unit's hard on new grads. You were a new grad. I know, Maria said. That's what I mean.
Lucia studied her own handwriting for a second. You still owe me the real one. From the essay. I know. When? When I can tell it all the way through.
That's not a date, Lucia said. Then she took the marker off the refrigerator and added a seventh row to the bottom of the matrix. Mom's story. She gave it the biggest weight on the page.
Thursday afternoon, May 13, Nate's team finished its first architecture review of Tributary. Maria was at her desk when his text came in.

A text from Nate Ostrowski. Read Tributary's disaster recovery plan, the one attached to our contract. Forty pages, and good ones. Last tested: never. Their failover has never once been run. Calling you in five.

Maria read it again, slower. The plan was an exhibit to a contract Cascade had signed two days ago. It said exactly what Tributary would do if its cloud went dark. Nobody, anywhere, had ever checked whether it was true.
Her phone rang at 4:57. How long to find out if it works? she said. Depends, Nate said. On whether they'll let us try.
